pairs.en: On the same day, the fourteenth of the month, we remember the holy prophet MICHAIAS.
*From the earth I was taken up; and if I reach the vault of heaven,* *Michaias will owe the favour to you, O tree.* *On the tenth and fourth, Michaias was raised upon a tree.*

This saint was one of the twelve prophets called the Minor Prophets, of the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Ioram, born in a place called Morathi, and he prophesied for eighty-four years, preceding the coming of Christ by six hundred and six years. Now because he kept rebuking Achab, the king of Samaria, for his many and various sins, he was hated by him; and since the prophet knew this, he withdrew and spent most of his time in the mountains, so that by continually appearing and rebuking the king he would not stir the king's anger to the point of killing him. After Achab died, the prophet rebuked Achab's son, named Ioram, for the unlawful things he did, which were like those of his father. But Ioram, being young, could not bear the prophet's rebuke; so he seized him and hanged him, and threw his remains into the ravine nearby. His kinsfolk took the body and buried it with honour in his homeland, called Morathi, near the cemetery of Enakeim. His tomb is known.

Note: Josephus says he was the son of Iemblios. Michaias was earlier than the prophet Elissaios. That is why Jeremiah mentions this Michaias by name, saying: “And men from among the elders of the land rose up, and said to all the assembly of the people: Michaias the Morathite lived in the days of Ezekias king of Judah, and he said to all the people of Judah: thus said the Lord — Sion shall be ploughed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become uninhabitable, and the mountain of the house shall become a wooded grove.” (Jeremiah 36, or by another numbering 26:17.) His prophecy was issued in the reigns of Ioatham, Achaz and Ezekias (see Clement the Canoniar).

Note also that this day is the forefeast of the Dormition of the Theotokos, and for this forefeast Saint Germanos of Constantinople has a homily, which begins: “He who is ever owing his own…” (It survives in the monastery of Dionysiou on the Holy Mountain.)

sections.heading: Holy Hieromartyr Marcellus, Bishop of Apameia

pairs.en: On the same day we remember the holy hieromartyr MARCELLOS, bishop of Apameia.
*Having sweetened God with the savours understood,* *you sweeten him with the savour of your flesh too, Father.*

This saint lived in the days of the emperor Theodosios the Great, in the year 379, and he came from Cyprus. When he was entrusted with civil authority there, he amazed everyone with the piety and righteousness with which he handled public affairs. Later he passed over to the order and office of the Church, and became bishop of Apameia, the city in Syria; and he lived justly and devoutly in his other dealings too. Above all, he proved a fervent champion of the faith of Christ, building churches and houses of God to the glory of God, and bringing the temples of the idols crashing down. But one of the idol temples, called the temple of Zeus, the demon who dwelt in it would not allow either to be burned or to be thrown down by any device. So the saint took water, blessed it, and sprinkled from it over the timbers that had been stacked inside the temple. Then, since the demon could no longer put any obstacle, the timbers caught fire and burned the temple down. This became the occasion for the idolaters to seize the saint and throw him into the fire; and in this way the man of blessed memory received the crown of martyrdom by fire. His gathering and feast is held at the church of the holy prophet, Forerunner and Baptist John, in a place called Phorachion.

Note that this account of Saint Marcellos is taken from the fifth book of the Ecclesiastical History of Theodoret of Cyrus, from its twenty-first chapter, where Theodoret tells these things at greater length: that Saint Marcellos, unable to throw that temple down — because its construction was solid, and its four columns could not be broken — asked God to reveal to him some way to bring it down. So a man was found who, though neither a builder nor a stone-cutter, was only used to carrying timbers on his shoulders; this man dug around three of the columns and put olive wood into the trenches. Then Theodoret says word for word: “So, having dug under three of the columns, he applied the flame to the wood. But a demon, appearing black, kept the wood from being consumed by the fire, as would naturally happen, and hindered the working of the flame. When they had done this many times and found the device unbeatable, they reported it to the shepherd (that is, to Saint Marcellos), who was resting at midday. He ran at once to the house of God, and having ordered water to be brought in a vessel, placed the water under the holy altar; and laying his face to the ground, he implored the loving Master not to give way any longer to the demon's tyranny, but to strip bare the demon's weakness and display His own power, lest the unbelievers take occasion from this for greater harm. Having said this and other things like it, and having made the sign of the Cross over the water, he ordered a certain Ekytios, a man honoured with the diaconate and fenced about with faith and zeal, to take the water, run quickly, sprinkle it in faith, and apply the flame. When this was done, the demon fled, unable to bear the assault of the water; and the fire, treating the hostile water like oil, seized upon the wood and consumed it all in an instant.”

Note also that from this deed of Saint Marcellos arose the custom of singing the Lesser Blessing of Waters on the first days of the month, and of sprinkling with the water the houses and places where sickness is found and demonic activity lodges, because that activity flees and is driven away by the blessed water. That water is blessed on other days too (apart, that is, from the day of Theophany) is witnessed by other Fathers as well: the godly Kyprianos (in his seventy-sixth letter), who says that the water of sprinkling is purifying, and the holy Epiphanios (in the twelfth heresy).

sections.heading: The Bringing-back of the Precious Cross to the Palace

pairs.en: We remember the bringing-back of the precious Cross to the palace.
*Having lit words in place of bright torches,* *I escort the Cross back within the palace walls.*

By “bringing-back of the Cross” is meant here the return of the precious wood of the Cross to the royal palace — the palace from which it used to set out on the thirty-first of July, as we said there, and was carried around the whole city until the fourteenth of this month.
We remember the holy martyr OURSIKIOS.
*The severed head of Oursikios, O Word of God —* *how could you ever leave it without a crown?*

This saint lived in the days of the emperor Maximian, in the year 300, and he came from the city of Siventos, which lies in Upper Illyria (that is, Slavonia), being a soldier by rank. Because he was a Christian, he was denounced to the emperor Maximian, who handed him over to the governor Aristeides to be judged by him. So they beat his back with oxhide whips and struck his sides hard; then they wrapped his hands in linen cloths soaked in oil, sprinkled sulphur and resin over them, and set fire to them. As the saint suffered these torments, he said that his hands suffered justly, because they had ransomed the tyrant who was going to perish miserably. Then the tyrant Maximian — having been accused by a certain Tertullianos who was present there, that once ransomed by the saint he had proved ungrateful to his benefactor — was put to shame by this, and ordered water to be poured over the martyr's hands to put out the fire. Seeing this, a pagan named Olbianos was seized by his anger and left the Praetorium; but on his way home he was bitten by a scorpion, and in great agony the wretch cast off his miserable soul. Saint Oursikios, having received the final sentence, was beheaded by a certain Oualens, the man who had denounced the saint earlier. Three times the inhuman man struck the saint's neck with the sword, and so the blessed one received the crown of martyrdom.

sections.heading: The Holy Martyr Lucius the Soldier

pairs.en: The holy martyr LUCIUS the soldier died by fire.
*Having fled the old leaven of error, Lucius,* *baked by the fire, you became new leavened bread for God.*

sections.heading: The Holy New Martyr Symeon of Trebizond

pairs.en: The holy new martyr SYMEON of Trebizond, who bore witness in Constantinople in the year 1653, died by hanging.
*A deep noose proved a step for Symeon,* *by which he ascended to the breadth of heaven.*
See his martyrdom in the New Martyrologion.
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
